name: James
author: Traditionally, this letter was written by James, a brother of Jesus, who did not follow him during his ministry but became a believer after the resurrection. He went on to lead the church in Jerusalem and was respected among Jewish believers for his devotion to God's law. He was killed in Jerusalem around AD 62. Some scholars think a later follower wrote in his name to honour his teaching. Others defend the traditional view.
audience: The letter is addressed to God's people scattered across the world. Traditionally this is taken to mean Jewish believers in Jesus living outside their homeland across the Roman world; some scholars think it describes all Christians, Jewish and Gentile alike, as God's people spread abroad. Many seem to have been poor, facing hardship and mistreatment, and sometimes pushed around by wealthy landowners and powerful neighbours.
era: If James wrote it, the letter likely dates from the 40s or 50s AD, making it one of the earliest Christian writings. Some scholars date it later in the first century. Judea and the surrounding lands were under Roman rule, with rising tension between Jews and their Roman governors. In many places a small group of rich landowners held most of the land, while ordinary people worked as day labourers or small farmers.

notes.2:1: Early believers met in gatherings James calls by the Greek word for 'synagogue', where rich and poor visitors could arrive side by side.
notes.2:14: Many scholars think this section answers people who had misunderstood Paul's teaching about faith; others think James wrote independently of Paul.
notes.4:13: Travelling merchants were common in the Roman world, moving between towns to trade for a season or a year.
notes.5:1: In this period wealthy landowners often hired day labourers for harvest, and workers depended on being paid each evening to feed their families.
notes.5:7: Farmers in the land of Israel depended on autumn rains to soften the ground for planting and spring rains to ripen the crops.
notes.5:13: Elders were the recognised leaders of a local church. Olive oil was widely used as a medicine and in prayer.

unsure.problem: 'Olive oil was widely used ... in prayer' is vague and doubtful. Oil was used to anoint people, as a medicine and as a religious sign, but saying it was 'widely used in prayer' may confuse readers. Also, the elders and oil appear at 5:14, not 5:13.
